title: An assembler, in two passes
task: Write `first_pass(text)`, which returns a dict of `{label: address}`, and `assemble(text)`, which returns a 32-word memory image: each instruction is `opcode << 5 | address`, and `DATA n` stores `n % 256`. Operands are numbers or labels. Raise `ValueError` for unknown instructions, undefined or duplicate labels, addresses outside 0–31, and programs over 32 words.
hints: `first_pass`: `addr = 0`, then `for line in text.splitlines(): label, name, _ = parse(line)`. If there's a label (and it's not already in the dict), set `labels[label] = addr`. If there's a name, `addr += 1`.

Write a helper `value(operand, labels)`: return 0 for `None`, `int(operand)` if it's a number, `labels[operand]` if it's a known label, and raise `ValueError` otherwise. Try `int()` first, and catch the `ValueError` it raises for a non-number.

In `assemble`, loop over the lines again, skipping any with no name. For `DATA`, append `value(...) % 256`. Otherwise, check that the name is in `OPCODES` and that `0 <= v < 32`, then append `OPCODES[name] << 5 | v`. Finally, raise if `len(words) > MEM_SIZE`, and return `words + [0] * (MEM_SIZE - len(words))`.

quiz.q: Why can't a one-pass assembler encode `JZ END` when END is defined further down?

options.text: END's address isn't known yet when the assembler reaches that line
options.why: That's a forward reference. The first pass counts addresses so every label is known before anything is encoded.
A jump can go to any address 0–31. The problem is the assembler's knowledge, not the CPU.

options.text: Labels have to be defined before the code that uses them
options.why: In this assembler they don't. Two passes are exactly what makes defining them later work.

quiz.q: A program is: a line with only `START:`, then `LOAD X`, `JZ END`, `HALT`, `END: HALT` and `X: DATA 0`. What address does END get?

options.why: START has no word of its own, so it names address 0. LOAD is 0, JZ is 1, HALT is 2, and END labels the HALT at 3.
That counts the `START:` line as a word. A label alone on its line doesn't take up memory.
Only instructions and DATA take up words. There are three before END.
